title: Reading the landscape: what the ground is telling you
description: Landforms keep a record of what made them: a U-shaped valley, a line of springs along a cliff, rock layers meeting at an angle. Each question shows a photo of real terrain and asks what happened there, and the explanation draws the cross-section. The route runs from glaciated mountains through rivers, limestone and desert to the coast, and ends at the Scottish outcrop where James Hutton saw deep time.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: This valley has a broad, flat floor and steep walls that curve up to meet it. What carved it into this shape?

images.alt: A wide valley between two steep, grassy mountainsides. Its floor is flat and farmed, and the walls curve smoothly down into it, giving the valley a rounded cross-section.
images.caption: Photo by Wilson44691, CC0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glacial_Valley_Ardara_Glengesh_Pass.jpg).

images.alt: Two cross-sections side by side. A river valley forms a sharp V with a small stream at the bottom point. A glaciated valley forms a rounded U filled almost to the brim with ice, with a dashed trimline above the ice surface.

options.text: A glacier that filled the valley and eroded its floor and walls together
A river that meandered back and forth for millions of years, widening the valley floor
A fault that dropped the valley floor down between two blocks of crust
Wind abrasion that sandblasted the lower slopes more than the upper ones

questions.explanation:
A river erodes only where its water flows, in a narrow strip along the bed. As it cuts down, the slopes on either side slump and wash in, leaving a **V**. A valley glacier is hundreds of metres thick and fills the valley to a high level. Rock frozen into its base scours the floor, and the same ice presses against the walls, so it widens and deepens the whole cross-section at once. The result is a **U**: steep sides, a flat floor, and often a trimline high on the walls where the ice surface used to be.

A meandering river can build a flat floor, but its valley sides stay gentle instead of curving steeply up. Valleys dropped between faults (grabens) usually have straight edges.

questions.title: This waterfall pours off the lip of a side valley that ends high above the main valley floor. Why does the side valley stop so abruptly?

images.alt: A tall, narrow waterfall drops from a notch high in a sheer granite cliff into a forested valley. The creek above it comes out of a smaller valley whose floor sits far above the main one.
images.caption: Photo by Brocken Inaglory, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:A_rainbow_over_Bridalveil_Fall_seen_from_Tunnel_View_in_Yosemite_NP.jpg).

images.alt: Cross-section of a small tributary glacier meeting a much larger trunk glacier. Both ice surfaces meet at the same height, but the trunk glacier's floor is far deeper. After the ice melts, the tributary stream falls off the resulting step as a waterfall.

options.text: A large trunk glacier deepened the main valley far more than the small glacier in the side valley could deepen its own floor
The side valley's stream is younger than the main river, so it has not yet had time to cut down
An earthquake lifted the side valley along a fault, leaving it stranded above the main floor
Harder rock in the side valley resisted a river that cut easily through soft rock in the main valley

questions.explanation:
This is Bridalveil Fall in Yosemite, which drops about 188 m from a **hanging valley**. During glaciations a thick trunk glacier filled Yosemite Valley, and smaller glaciers fed into it from the side valleys. Their ice surfaces joined at roughly the same level, but a thicker, faster glacier erodes harder, so the trunk glacier ground its floor down much further than the small tributary could.

While the ice was there, you couldn't see the difference. Once it melted, the side valley was left perched on a cliff, and its stream now falls off the step. Rivers alone rarely do this. Where a tributary joins a river, the two floors usually meet at the same level, because the smaller stream cuts down to match the one it flows into.

questions.title: From the summit of Helvellyn you look down on a round lake in a steep-walled bowl, beside a knife-edged ridge. What can you read from this view?

images.alt: A small, nearly round dark lake lying in a deep bowl with steep grassy and rocky back walls. To the right, a narrow, jagged ridge runs away from the viewer along the rim of the bowl.
images.caption: Photo by Tim Stevens, CC BY 2.5, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Striding_Edge_and_Red_Tarn,_Helvellyn.jpg).

options.text: The bowl is a cirque, cut where a small glacier started at the head of a valley
The lake sits in a hollow that the ice dug below the level of the bowl's rim
The sharp ridge was left standing as ice ate into it from both sides
The bowl is the crater of an extinct volcano
The ridge is a pile of rubble that a glacier dumped at its edge

questions.explanation:
Snow collects in a sheltered hollow and turns to ice, and the ice starts to rotate slowly downhill. Along the back wall it plucks rock away, so the wall grows steeper. Beneath it, the rotating ice scrapes the floor down into a basin. The result is an armchair-shaped **cirque**, and the rock lip at its mouth often holds water once the ice melts. That lake is a **tarn**, in this case Red Tarn.

When two cirques cut back toward each other, the rock between them narrows to a knife-edge called an **arête**. Striding Edge is one of the best-known in Britain. Helvellyn's rocks are volcanic, formed about 450 million years ago, which makes the crater option tempting. But this bowl was cut by ice long after any volcano had gone. A dumped rubble ridge would be a moraine, which is soft and rounded. An arête is bare bedrock, sharpened from both sides.

questions.title: This bare rock hump has one long, smooth, gently rising side and one short, steep side broken into blocks. Glaciers made it. Which way was the ice moving?

images.alt: A pale grey bedrock hump in a grassy mountain valley. Its left side rises in a long, smooth, rounded slope; its right end is shorter, steeper, and broken into angular, jagged blocks.
images.caption: Photo by Jynto, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Roche_Moutonn%C3%A9e_Cadair_Idris.jpg).

images.alt: Cross-section of a rock hump under a dashed ice surface, with ice flowing left to right. The gentle left slope is labelled stoss side, smoothed and scratched. The steep right end is labelled lee side, with blocks plucked away.

options.text: Up the smooth side and over the top, toward the steep, broken side
Up the steep, broken side and over the top, toward the smooth side
Along the length of the hump, parallel to both sides
You cannot tell; the ice shapes both sides the same way

questions.explanation:
This is a **roche moutonnée**. Where ice pushes against a rock obstacle, stones frozen into the glacier base grind the up-ice (**stoss**) side smooth and scratch it with striations. Over the top, pressure drops. Meltwater seeps into cracks on the down-ice (**lee**) side and refreezes onto the moving ice, which then pulls whole blocks away. That process is called plucking, and it leaves a steep, jagged face.

So the polished slope faces the direction the ice came from, and the broken face points where it went. Hold on to this one: a drumlin, a few Questions on, has the opposite profile.

questions.title: Low, smooth hills like this one come in swarms, all stretched the same way. Each has a steep, blunt end and a long, tapering tail. What shaped them, and which way does the blunt end face?

images.alt: A long, low, grass-topped island rising from a flat sandy shore, with rippled sand in the foreground. The island is smoothly elongated, with a steeper, higher end on one side and a gentler slope on the other.
images.caption: Photo by Brendanconway, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Drowned_drumlin_in_Clew_Bay.jpg).

images.alt: Side view of a drumlin made of till, with ice flowing left to right. The steep, blunt end is on the left, facing up-ice, and a long tapering tail runs to the right, down-ice.

options.text: Moving ice molded them from sediment, and the blunt end faces the direction the ice came from
Moving ice molded them from sediment, and the blunt end faces the direction the ice went
Wind piled them up as dunes, and the blunt end faces downwind
Rivers cut them out of an old plain, and the blunt end faces upstream

questions.explanation:
These are **drumlins**. This one, in Clew Bay in Ireland, was partly drowned by the rising sea. Drumlins are made of **till**: the unsorted clay, sand and stones a glacier drags along its bed. Ice flowing over that sediment smears it into streamlined hills whose long axes line up with the flow, which is why they come in swarms that all point the same way.

The steep end usually faces **up-ice**, and the tail stretches out down-ice. That is the reverse of a roche moutonnée, where the gentle side faces the ice. A simple way to remember it: a drumlin is built of soft sediment, so it gets streamlined like a teardrop, blunt end first. A roche moutonnée is solid rock, so the ice rounds its upstream face and quarries its downstream one. A dune also has one steep side, but it faces downwind, and dunes aren't made of mixed clay and boulders.

questions.title: A road runs for kilometres along the crest of this narrow, winding ridge, with lakes on both sides. Its core is layers of sand and gravel. What built it?

images.alt: Aerial view of a long, narrow, pine-covered ridge snaking across a large lake, with water close on both sides and a road running along its crest into the distance.
images.caption: Photo by Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Punkaharju_esker_towards_Pentinniemi_in_Savonlinna,_Southern_Savonia,_Finland,_2022_June.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. Left: a meltwater tunnel at the base of a glacier, partly filled with layered sand and gravel. Right: after the ice melts, the same sand and gravel stands as a rounded ridge called an esker.

options.text: A meltwater river flowing in a tunnel under the ice, which filled its own channel with sediment
The front edge of a glacier, which bulldozed loose rock into a ridge as it advanced
Lake waves that built a long sandbar out from the shore
A lava flow that later weathered down into sand and gravel

questions.explanation:
This is the Punkaharju ridge in Finland, an **esker**. Under a melting ice sheet, meltwater collects into rivers that flow through tunnels in and beneath the ice. Walls of ice hold the tunnel in place, so the river piles sand and gravel on its bed until the channel is choked. When the ice melts away, the sediment stays behind as a ridge in the shape of the old channel.

Two clues point to running water rather than ice. The sediment is **sorted and layered**, and eskers **wind** like the rivers that made them, sometimes for hundreds of kilometres. Because the water was under pressure, an esker can even climb gently uphill in places. Material bulldozed by an ice front would form a moraine, a jumble of every grain size across the valley. A sandbar would run along a shoreline, not wind across a lake. Eskers make well-drained, level routes, which is why so many carry roads and railways.

questions.title: This hummocky ridge near New Zealand's Tasman Glacier is strewn with boulders of every size, from pebbles to blocks as big as sheep. What can you conclude about it?

images.alt: A grassy, hummocky slope under a blue sky, scattered with grey boulders of many different sizes, from small stones to large blocks, lying at random.
images.caption: Photo by Krzysztof Golik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Terminal_moraine_of_Tasman_Glacier.jpg).

options.text: It was dumped by ice, which carries everything from clay to boulders and drops it all together
It marks a line where a glacier's front stood still long enough to pile up debris
Ridges like this often hold back a lake once the glacier retreats behind them
Its material was sorted into layers by running water
It formed under the glacier, streamlined by the ice flowing over it

questions.explanation:
The giveaway is **no sorting**. Water and wind sort sediment, because at any speed they can move grains up to a certain size and no bigger. Ice can carry a boulder and a clay particle side by side. When it melts, it drops them together, as unsorted **till**.

A glacier works like a conveyor belt. Even when its front holds still, ice keeps flowing forward and melting, and debris piles up at the margin as a **moraine** ridge. A terminal moraine marks the farthest point the ice reached. When the glacier retreats, the ridge often acts as a dam, and the Tasman Glacier's own meltwater lake sits behind moraines like this one.

Sorted, layered gravel would point to meltwater, as in an esker. A streamlined hill shaped beneath the ice would be a drumlin, and that shape would line up with the ice flow, not run across the valley.

questions.title: This lone granite boulder sits in a Connecticut wood. What would best show that ice carried it here, rather than it rolling downhill or weathering out on the spot?

images.alt: A large, grey, speckled granite boulder, taller than a person, resting on leaf litter among small trees, with a few much smaller stones around its base.
images.caption: Photo by Marty Aligata, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Glacial_Erratic_in_Ledyard,_CT.jpg).

options.text: It is a different rock type from the bedrock beneath it, and matching outcrops lie many kilometres away in the direction the ice came from
It is far larger than any other stone nearby, too big for a stream to have moved
Its corners are rounded off, as if it had been tumbled a long way
Thick moss and lichen cover it, so it has sat there for thousands of years

questions.explanation:
A **glacial erratic** is identified by what it is made of, not by its size or shape. Geologists compare the boulder with the bedrock underneath. If they don't match, it came from somewhere else. If a matching outcrop lies up-ice, and there is no slope or river that could have moved it, ice is the only carrier left. Erratics traced this way helped convince 19th-century geologists that ice sheets once covered northern Europe and North America.

Size alone proves nothing. A local outcrop can weather into big blocks, and rockfalls deliver huge boulders downhill. Rounding happens in rivers and on beaches too. A coat of lichen only tells you the surface has been exposed for a while.

questions.title: Below these cliffs, loose rock has built up into long, straight-sided slopes of scree. Where on a scree slope do you usually find the biggest blocks?

images.alt: Jagged, grey rock cliffs rising above long, smooth, fan-shaped slopes of loose grey rubble that spread down to a flat, green valley floor with a few buildings.
images.caption: Photo by Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Losar_Spiti_Scree_Left_Himachal_Jun18_D72_7825.jpg).

options.text: At the foot, because big blocks carry more momentum and roll past the smaller stones
At the top, because big blocks are too heavy to move far from the cliff
In the middle, where the slope is steepest
Scattered evenly, because rockfall is random

questions.explanation:
This scree is in Spiti, in the Indian Himalaya. Water freezes in cracks in the cliff and expands by about 9%, and repeated freeze-thaw prises blocks loose until they fall. Each new piece bounces and rolls down the pile. Small fragments lose their momentum quickly and lodge in gaps near the top. Big blocks carry more momentum, roll over the small stuff, and end up at the bottom. So, oddly, the heaviest pieces travel furthest, and scree slopes are usually well sorted, with the coarsest blocks at the foot.

The straight profile comes from the **angle of repose**, the steepest angle at which loose rock stays put, usually somewhere in the 30s of degrees. Add more rubble on top and the excess slides until the slope drops back to that angle. Slopes that are no longer being fed usually relax to a gentler, slightly concave profile.

questions.title: At Weeping Rock in Zion, water drips from one level across an overhanging cliff, and ferns grow in a band along it. What can you conclude from where the water comes out?

images.alt: A curved, overhanging sandstone alcove streaked with dark water stains. Water drips from a line near its base, where a band of green plants hangs along the rock above a railed walkway with visitors.
images.caption: Photo by Elin Beckmann, CC BY 2.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Weeping_Rock,_Zion.jpg).

images.alt: Cross-section of porous sandstone lying above a less permeable siltstone and mudstone layer. Arrows show water sinking down through the sandstone, then turning sideways along the top of the lower layer and seeping out at the cliff face, where an alcove forms.

options.text: A rock that lets water through lies on top of one that lets water through far less easily
The water fell as rain or snow on the plateau above and soaked down through the rock
The seeps line up because they all come out at the same boundary between rock layers
The upper rock must be watertight, so rain runs off its surface and down the cliff
The water is being pushed up from the river at the canyon floor

questions.explanation:
Water sinks through a permeable rock until it reaches a layer it can't easily enter. It then spreads sideways along the top of that layer and comes out wherever the boundary meets the surface. Springs therefore line up along a **spring line** that follows the contact between the two rocks.

In Zion, the upper rock is the Navajo Sandstone, cemented dune sand that the park service describes as "porous like a sponge". Below it lie the siltstones and mudstones of the Kayenta Formation, which pass water far less readily. Rain and snowmelt soak into the plateau and emerge at the contact. The wet rock crumbles, the alcove grows, and ferns and other plants form a hanging garden in the constant drip.

The same logic explains the spring-line villages along the foot of England's chalk downs. Chalk lies over clay, and the villages grew where the water comes out.

questions.title: Malham Cove is an 80-metre curved limestone cliff with a dry lip. A stream flows out of a cave at its foot, and on the moor above, about a mile away, another stream disappears into the ground. What does this tell you about limestone country?

images.alt: A huge, pale grey, curved limestone cliff rising above a grassy valley with a drystone wall. A darker vertical streak runs down the middle of the cliff face beneath a dry notch in its lip.
images.caption: Photo by F. C. Franklin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Malham_Cove_1.jpg).

images.alt: Cross-section of layered limestone. A stream on the moor sinks into a crack and flows underground through dissolved channels, emerging at the foot of the cliff. The cliff's lip, marked as an old waterfall, is now dry.

options.text: Rainwater, made slightly acidic by dissolved carbon dioxide, widens cracks in limestone into underground channels
Rivers can disappear at the surface and come back out somewhere else entirely
A valley can stay dry even though a river once flowed through it
The cliff's dry lip means the local climate is too dry for rivers today
The stream at the foot must be the same water that sank nearest the cliff

questions.explanation:
Rain picks up carbon dioxide from the air and soil and becomes a weak carbonic acid. Limestone dissolves in it. Over thousands of years, water widens joints and bedding planes into fissures and caves. Surface streams find these openings and sink, a hallmark of **karst** landscapes.

Malham Cove shows the whole story. At the end of the last Ice Age, when the ground was frozen and the cracks sealed, a huge waterfall of meltwater poured over this lip. Today the water goes underground before it reaches the edge, leaving the lip dry. The dark streak marks where the fall once ran. The climate is still wet; the water has simply found a route underground.

The last option is a trap. Dye tests showed that the stream sinking at Water Sinks, near Malham Tarn, does *not* feed the stream at the cove's foot. It comes out at Aire Head, south of the village. The two flows cross behind the cliff without mixing. Underground drainage in karst rarely follows the surface map.

questions.title: This crater opened in an Alabama wood in 1972, apparently all at once. There is limestone underneath and a thick layer of clay on top. Why can a hole like this appear so suddenly?

images.alt: Black-and-white aerial photo of a large, steep-walled oval hole in a forest, with bare, collapsed walls and a pool of water at the bottom.
images.caption: Photo by T. V. Stone, USGS, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:December_Giant_sinkhole_collapse_USGS_1972.jpg).

images.alt: Three panels of clay over limestone. First, a small void opens where grains wash down into a limestone cavity. Second, the void grows upward as a thin clay arch while the surface still looks normal. Third, the roof fails and the surface drops into a steep-sided hole.

options.text: Sticky clay bridged a cavity that grew upward out of sight, until the thin roof could no longer hold
The limestone bedrock dissolved in a single wet season
An underground gas explosion blew out the crater
A small meteorite impact that left no fragments

questions.explanation:
This is a **cover-collapse sinkhole**, and it forms from below. Water moving down through cracks in the limestone washes clay and sand into the voids underneath. A cavity opens at the base of the clay. Clay is cohesive, so it arches over the hole the way a stone bridge spans a gap, and the cavity migrates upward as its roof keeps spalling. At the surface nothing seems to change, until the last thin layer gives way.

The limestone dissolved over thousands of years; only the final failure was fast. A USGS report on human-induced sinkholes opens with this photo and calls it the largest collapse in Alabama. That report explains a common trigger: pumping groundwater lowers the water table and takes away the buoyancy that was helping to hold the clay up. That is why sinkholes cluster around wells, quarries and dewatered mines.
questions.references: [USGS Circular 968: Development of sinkholes resulting from man's activities in the eastern United States](https://pubs.usgs.gov/circ/1987/0968/report.pdf) · [Wikipedia: Sinkhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinkhole)

questions.title: Look at any loop of this river: one bank is a gentle bar of gravel and sand, and the other is a steep, eroding edge. Which statements about a river bend are true?

images.alt: A green river valley seen from a mountainside. A wide river swings through broad loops, with pale gravel bars on the inside of the bends and forested banks on the outside.
images.caption: Photo by Walter Siegmund, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Skagit_River_8667s.JPG).

images.alt: Cross-section of a river bend. The outer bank is a steep cut bank with the deepest, fastest water against it. The inner bank slopes gently up as a point bar of sand and gravel deposited in slow water.

options.text: The steep, eroding bank is on the outside of the bend
The deepest water runs close to the outer bank
Sand and gravel settle on the inside of the bend, where the water slows
Over time the bend moves toward its inner bank
The water flows fastest along the inner bank because it has less distance to travel

questions.explanation:
As water rounds a bend, its momentum carries the fastest flow toward the outside. There it scours the bed deepest and undercuts the bank, which collapses into a steep **cut bank**. On the inside, the water is shallow and slow. It can't hold its coarser sediment, so it drops it as a sloping **point bar**. A corkscrew-shaped (helical) current also sweeps sediment across the bed from the outer bank toward the inner one.

Erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside mean the whole bend migrates **outward** and slowly downstream. Loops keep growing until something cuts them off, which is the next Question. This view shows the Skagit River in Washington, with pale gravel bars on the inner side of its bends.

questions.title: From the air, this river is surrounded by crescent-shaped lakes whose curves match the river's own loops. How did they get cut off?

images.alt: Aerial view of a flat, wet plain with a winding river whose pale sandbars trace tight loops. Around it lie many crescent- and horseshoe-shaped lakes and faint curved scars matching the river's bends.
images.caption: Photo by katorisi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Oxbow_lake,Yamal_Peninsula,Russia.JPG).

images.alt: Three stages of a river loop. First, the outer banks of a tight loop erode toward each other and the neck narrows. Second, a flood breaks through the neck and the water takes the short cut. Third, sediment seals both ends of the abandoned loop, leaving a crescent lake.

options.text: Loops grew until two bends nearly met, then the river broke through the narrow neck and sealed off the old loop
Each lake is a separate kettle hole left by a buried block of glacier ice
Beavers dammed the river at many points, backing water into its old bends
The ground sank along curved faults beside the river

questions.explanation:
Meander bends grow outward, as the previous Question showed. On a tight loop, the outer banks on either side of the **neck** erode toward each other. Eventually a flood breaks through, often during high water, and the river takes the short, steep route. The old loop now carries almost no flow. Sediment settles at both ends where it meets the river, sealing the loop into an **oxbow lake**.

That is why these lakes keep the exact curve and width of a river channel. Kettle lakes are roughly round and scattered at random. Here, on the Yamal Peninsula in Arctic Russia, you can see every stage: live loops, fresh cutoffs, and older crescents fading into faint scars as they fill with silt and plants.

questions.title: This shaded-relief map shows a river valley in Japan (green is low, orange is high). The valley sides rise in a staircase of flat steps. Which step is the oldest?

images.alt: A colour shaded-relief elevation map. Two green valleys join in a Y. On both sides, the land rises in several broad, flat, sharply edged steps, shaded from green at the valley floor through yellow to orange on the high ground.
images.caption: Photo by Batholith, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:River_terraces,_Numata,_Gunma,_Japan.jpg).

images.alt: Cross-section of a valley with three pairs of flat steps on each side above today's river. The highest step is labelled oldest, the next younger, and the lowest younger still, just above today's river channel.

options.text: The highest step, farthest above today's river
The lowest step, closest to today's river
They formed at the same time, as one flood deposit that later cracked into steps
The river channel itself, because the river was there first

questions.explanation:
Each flat step is a **river terrace**: a former floodplain. A river builds a floodplain at its own level. If the land rises, the sea level falls, or the climate changes the river's load, the river starts **cutting down**. The old floodplain is left high and dry as a terrace, and a new floodplain forms at the lower level. Repeat that, and you get a staircase.

The river can only abandon a surface above it, so the **highest terrace is the oldest**, and each lower step is younger. That reverses the usual rule of stacked sediment, where the bottom layer is the oldest. Terraces aren't stacked; they're cut into each other. The present channel is the youngest feature of all. This site is Numata in Gunma Prefecture, Japan, whose terrace staircase is especially well developed.

questions.title: Seen from above, where each canyon opens onto Death Valley's flat floor, a cone of gravel spreads out. Why does the sediment pile up right at the canyon mouth?

images.alt: View from a high ridge down a steep, eroded desert canyon. Beyond, on the flat valley floor, a broad, pale, fan-shaped apron of sediment spreads out from the base of the mountains.
images.caption: Photo by Wilson44691, CC0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Death_Valley_Alluvial_Fan_from_Dante%27s_View.JPG).

images.alt: A narrow canyon opening onto a flat plain. Arrows show the flow spreading out, slowing, and soaking into gravel. Large boulders lie near the apex of the fan, grading to small sand and silt grains at its toe.

options.text: The confined flow spreads out, gets shallower and slower, and soaks into the ground, so it can no longer carry its load
The wind blows fine sediment back toward the mountains, where it piles against their base
The canyon mouth is the lowest point in the valley, so everything drains and collects there
Rockfall from the canyon walls tumbles out and lands in a cone at the entrance

questions.explanation:
In a canyon, a flash flood is squeezed into a narrow channel, so it runs deep and fast and can move boulders. At the mountain front the walls end. The water spreads sideways, gets shallow, slows, and sinks into dry gravel. Its carrying capacity collapses, so it drops its load right there. The biggest pieces fall first near the apex, and finer sand and silt travel further out to the toe.

Each flood shifts to a new path across the pile, so over time the deposit grows into a symmetrical cone: an **alluvial fan**. The lowest point of Death Valley is out on the salt flats, far from the canyon mouths, so the fan sits where the flow changed, not where the ground is lowest. Rockfall builds scree cones directly under cliffs, not smooth fans reaching kilometres onto the valley floor.

questions.title: This fresh step in the ground appeared in a single morning in 1983, running for kilometres along the foot of Idaho's Lost River Range. What made it?

images.alt: Black-and-white photo of a sagebrush plain crossed by a sharp, raw step in the ground with a crumbling face, running in a straight line into the distance.
images.caption: Photo by R. E. Wallace, USGS, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fault_Scarp_Borah_Peak_Earthquake_1983.jpg).

images.alt: Cross-section of a normal fault. The crust is pulled apart and the hanging-wall block slides down along an inclined fault plane, leaving a fresh step, the scarp, where the fault meets the surface. The footwall stays higher.

options.text: An earthquake, when the ground on one side of a fault dropped down relative to the other
A landslide that slumped away from the mountain front after heavy rain
Erosion along the bank of an old stream channel that has since dried up
Soil that shrank and cracked open during a long drought

questions.explanation:
This is a **fault scarp** from the magnitude 6.9 Borah Peak earthquake of 28 October 1983. The Basin and Range region is being stretched. When accumulated strain on the Lost River Fault released, the valley-side block slid down the inclined fault plane, relative to the mountain side. The ground broke along a zone about 34 km long, with a throw of up to about 2.7 m.

Two things mark a fault rather than a landslide or a stream. The step runs **straight across the terrain**, ignoring ridges and gullies, because it follows a plane cutting down into the crust. And the same fault has moved many times before: the whole mountain range is the sum of thousands of these steps.

questions.title: Inside this sandstone, thin layers are stacked in sets, and within each set they tilt the same way before being cut off by the set above. What made these tilted layers?

images.alt: Close view of pink and cream sandstone with small shrubs. Thin, closely spaced layers sweep across the rock at an angle in several stacked sets, each set truncated at its top by the next.
images.caption: Photo by Zion National Park, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sandstone_Cross-bedding_%285930953092%29.jpg).

images.alt: A dune with wind blowing left to right. Grains hop up the gentle windward side and avalanche down the steep lee face, building inclined layers. Below, the same pattern is shown as rock: stacked sets of inclined layers, all dipping downwind, each set's top cut off by the next.

options.text: Migrating sand dunes, with each tilted layer marking a sand avalanche down the dune's downwind face
Earth movements that tilted flat layers after they had hardened
Ocean waves washing sand up and down a beach
Mud cracks that filled with sand

questions.explanation:
This is **cross-bedding** in Zion's Navajo Sandstone, a desert sea of dunes turned to stone about 190 million years ago. Wind rolls and bounces grains up the gentle windward side of a dune. When the crest gets too steep, sand avalanches down the lee face, laying down a thin layer inclined at up to about 30–34°. As the dune advances, it buries layer after layer of these slopes.

When the next dune passes over, it planes off the top of the old one. That is why each set is truncated. The layers **dip downwind**, so geologists measure them to map ancient wind directions. The tilting happened as the sand was laid down, not later: a later tilt would rotate every layer, including the boundaries between sets, by the same amount.

questions.title: Monument Valley's buttes stand alone on a flat desert, each with a flat top and vertical sides. Why does erosion leave them this shape?

images.alt: A tall, flat-topped red rock tower with sheer vertical walls rising from a sloping skirt of rubble, standing alone on a flat red desert with scrubby bushes and a dead tree in front.
images.caption: Photo by Tobi 87, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monument_Valley_West_Mitten_Butte.jpg).

images.alt: Three stages side by side: a wide mesa, a narrower butte and a thin spire, each topped by a thin layer of hard caprock over softer red layers, standing on slopes of weak shale.

options.text: A tough layer on top protects the rock below, while weaker layers underneath wear back and undercut the cliffs, so the walls retreat without lowering the top
They are the necks of ancient volcanoes, whose hardened lava resisted erosion better than the rock around it
Sand-laden wind cut their sides vertical, but only up to the height the blown sand could reach
They are ancient reefs that grew straight upward from a shallow sea floor

questions.explanation:
The rock here is flat-lying layers of different strength. A hard **caprock** on top resists weathering from above, so the summit stays flat. The cliffs retreat sideways instead. Weaker beds lower down crumble into sloping aprons, undercutting the stronger rock above, which breaks off along vertical joints. The walls stay steep as they back away.

Over time a broad **mesa** shrinks to a **butte**, then to a narrow spire, and finally to nothing. The flat tops of Monument Valley's buttes line up at roughly the same height because they are remnants of one continuous plateau. Volcanic necks, like Shiprock in New Mexico, are made of solidified magma and look very different: jagged, not layered.

questions.title: In this canyon wall, pale pink bands slice straight across the dark, streaky rock. Which formed first?

images.alt: A steep, dark grey rock wall with faint streaky layering, crossed by several pale pink bands that run at angles across it, some branching and cutting through each other.
images.caption: Photo by Daniel Mayer (Mav), CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Black_Canyon_of_the_Gunnison_National_Park_in_September_2011_-_dikes_in_canyon_wall.JPG).

images.alt: Dark rock with wavy layering, cut by two orange bands of once-molten rock labelled younger. Captions: first the dark rock forms and is folded, then magma forces into cracks across it.

options.text: The dark rock; the pink bands formed later when molten rock forced its way into cracks through it
The pink bands; the dark rock was deposited around them later, filling the spaces between
Both at once, as a single cooling rock separated into light and dark minerals
You can't tell the order without laboratory dating

questions.explanation:
The **principle of cross-cutting relationships** says a feature that cuts across a rock must be younger than the rock it cuts. You can't slice through something that doesn't exist yet. The pink bands here are **dikes**, sheets of once-molten rock (mostly pegmatite) that squeezed into fractures in the older dark metamorphic rock of the Black Canyon of the Gunnison, Colorado, and crystallised there.

The same rule works on dikes that cross each other: the one that goes straight through is younger than the one it interrupts. Nicolas Steno and later James Hutton turned simple rules like this into a way of putting events in order long before anyone could put numbers on them. That is called relative dating, and it needs no laboratory.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Cross-cutting relationships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-cutting_relationships) · [Wikipedia: Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Canyon_of_the_Gunnison_National_Park)

questions.title: The Giant's Causeway is a pavement of tightly fitting stone columns, mostly six-sided. What made them?

images.alt: Close-up of the flat tops of dark stone columns fitting together like paving, most with five or six straight sides, with grass growing in the narrow joints between them.
images.caption: Photo by Suzanne Mischyshyn, CC BY-SA 2.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:County_Antrim_-_Giant%27s_Causeway_-_Tops_of_Basalt_Columns_-_geograph.org.uk_-_3987884.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. Side view of a cooling lava flow with cracks growing inward from its top and base toward a dashed line in the middle. Top view of a honeycomb of hexagonal columns.

options.text: A thick lava flow shrank as it cooled and cracked into a network of columns
Each column is a single giant crystal that grew from the lava
Waves eroded the rock along a regular pattern of weaknesses left by earthquakes
Sediment filled the cells of an ancient coral reef and hardened

questions.explanation:
About 50 to 60 million years ago, fluid basalt lava ponded here in thick flows. Rock contracts as it cools, so the flow surfaces shrank but were held in place and cracked, much as drying mud does. Once started, the cracks grew into the flow at right angles to the cooling surfaces, from the top down and the bottom up. They split the lava into long parallel **columns**.

A crack network relieves stress most efficiently when cracks meet at about 120°, so hexagons dominate. They are not perfect: the columns here have between four and eight sides, which a crystal would not allow. The columns are fine-grained basalt made of many tiny crystals, not one giant one.

questions.title: Off this chalk headland, a big block has a tunnel through its base, and a lone pillar stands further out. What was the lone pillar before it stood alone?

images.alt: Brilliant white chalk rising from blue sea: a large, grass-topped block with a dark cave and arch hollowed through its base, and a separate, narrower chalk pillar standing a little way out to sea.
images.caption: Photo by Chris Downer, CC BY-SA 2.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Old_Harry_and_Handfast_Point_-_geograph.org.uk_-_499665.jpg).

images.alt: Five panels of a rock headland in the sea: a crack, then a cave at water level, then an arch through the rock, then a stack standing alone beside a thin remnant, then a low stump.

options.text: Part of an arch, whose roof collapsed after waves hollowed a cave right through the headland
An island that was always separate and has been rising out of the sea
A column of harder rock that never belonged to the headland
A pile of fallen blocks that the waves cemented together

questions.explanation:
These are Old Harry Rocks on the Dorset coast in England. Waves attack a headland from both sides, forcing water and air into joints (hydraulic action) and grinding with sand and pebbles. A weak joint becomes a **cave**. Caves from each side meet, or one punches straight through, to form an **arch**. Weakened from below and weathered from above, the arch roof eventually falls, leaving the seaward end standing alone as a **stack**. Undercut at its base, the stack later topples to a **stump** covered at high tide.

This photo shows several stages at once: the big block is an arch in the making, and Old Harry himself is the stack. The chalk here once ran unbroken to the Needles on the Isle of Wight. Old Harry's original "wife", a neighbouring stack, is recorded as having fallen in 1509.

questions.title: At Siccar Point in Scotland, grey rock layers stand almost vertical, and flatter red sandstone lies across their eroded tops. Why do the two sets meet at an angle?

images.alt: A rocky shore where grey rock layers stand nearly upright like ribs. Resting on their worn, flattened tops is a gently sloping cap of reddish sandstone layers.
images.caption: Photo by Lysippos, CC BY 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hutton%27s_unconformity_siccar_point.JPG).

images.alt: Four panels: grey layers laid down flat; the same layers tilted upright into folds; their tops eroded flat; then new red layers deposited horizontally across the eroded surface. A red line marks the eroded surface as the gap in time.

options.text: The grey layers were laid down flat, tilted upright by mountain building, worn down, and then buried under new sand much later
The grey layers settled vertically against a steep underwater slope and have stayed that way ever since
The red sandstone was shoved sideways over the grey rock along a low-angle fault, grinding their contact flat
Both sets formed together, and the grey rock later shrank and cracked into vertical slabs

questions.explanation:
Sediment settles in flat layers, so vertical layers mean something turned them. About 435 million years ago, mud and sand accumulated in flat beds on the floor of an ancient ocean. The ocean closed, and the collision of continents crumpled those beds until they stood nearly upright. Over the following tens of millions of years, erosion planed their tops flat. Then, around 370 million years ago, rivers and wind spread red sand across that surface. That sand became the Old Red Sandstone.

The boundary between the two, an **angular unconformity**, represents about **65 million years** missing from the record. James Hutton was shown it by boat in 1788 and took it as proof that Earth's history is almost unimaginably long. His companion John Playfair wrote that "the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time."

questions.title: You're walking an unfamiliar landscape. Which of these finds, taken alone, tell you that glaciers once covered it?
questions.description: Every landform here appeared earlier in this Quiz.

options.text: A swarm of streamlined till hills, all stretched the same way
A long, winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel crossing low ground
A boulder of rock found nowhere in the bedrock around it
A side valley whose floor ends at a cliff high above the main valley
A crescent-shaped lake beside a looping river
A cone of gravel spreading from a canyon mouth
A straight, fresh step running across hillsides

questions.explanation:
Drumlins, eskers, erratics and hanging valleys all need ice. Drumlins are till molded beneath moving ice. Eskers are the sediment of rivers that ran in tunnels under it. Erratics are rocks carried far from home, often uphill, which only ice does. A hanging valley records a trunk glacier deepening its floor far below its tributaries.

The other three form without ice. Oxbow lakes come from any meandering river. Alluvial fans need only a canyon, a flat plain, and occasional floods, and deserts are full of them. A straight fresh step across terrain is a fault scarp, made by an earthquake. Several of these can sit beside ice-age landforms, since rivers and faults don't stop when the ice leaves. But on their own, they say nothing about glaciers.
